title: Of managing the will
paragraphs: Few things, compared with what commonly affect other people, move me — or, more accurately, take possession of me. It is reasonable that things should concern a man, provided they do not occupy him entirely. I work hard, by study and argument, to enlarge this privilege of insensibility, which is already pretty well developed in me by nature, so that as a consequence I take up and feel strongly about very few things. My sight is clear enough, but I fix it on very few objects; my senses are delicate and tender enough, but my grasp and engagement are hard and slack. I am very reluctant to engage myself; as far as in me lies, I employ myself wholly on myself, and even in that subject I would rather rein in my attachment than let it plunge over its head, since the self is a subject I hold at the mercy of others, and over which fortune has more right than I do. So even with health, which I value so highly, it is all the more necessary for me not to crave and obsess over it as passionately as I find diseases unbearable. A man ought to find a middle ground between the hatred of pain and the love of pleasure, and Plato sets out a middle path of life between the two. But against the affections that carry me wholly out of myself and fix me elsewhere — those I oppose with all the force I have. My opinion is that a man should lend himself to others, but only give himself to himself. If my will were easy to lend out or to be swayed, I would not last long; I am too tender, both by nature and habit.
"Fugax rerum, securaque in otia natus."
["Avoiding affairs and born to secure ease." --Ovid, De Trist., iii. 2, 9.]

Hot and stubborn disputes in which my opponent would end up winning, where the outcome would make my heat and obstinacy look ridiculous, would perhaps annoy me beyond bearing. If I threw myself into things at the rate others do, my soul would never have the strength to sustain the agitation and alarms of those who grasp at so much; it would be disordered at once by the inner turmoil. When I have at times been put in charge of other men's affairs, I have promised to take them in hand, but not into my lungs and liver — to take them up, not to absorb them — to work at them, yes; to get worked up about them, no. I attend to them, but I will not brood over them. I have enough on my hands to order and govern the domestic crowd inside my own veins and bowels without bringing a crowd of other men's affairs in too; and I have enough natural and personal business of my own without meddling in other people's. Those who know how much they owe to themselves, and how many duties of their own they are bound to, find that nature has cut out work enough to keep them from being idle. "You have business enough at home: look to that."

Men let themselves out for hire; their faculties are not for themselves but for those to whom they have enslaved themselves; their tenants occupy them, not they themselves. This common humour does not suit me. We must be thrifty with the liberty of our souls, and only let it out for genuine occasions, which are very few when we judge rightly. Just observe those who have got into the habit of being at everyone's beck and call: they do it indifferently for any occasion, large or small, in matters that do not concern them at all as much as in those that concern them most. They throw themselves indifferently into anywhere there is work to be done and an obligation, and they are lifeless when they are not in some noisy bustle.
"In negotiis sunt, negotii causa,"
["They are in business for business' sake."--Seneca, Ep., 22.]

It is not so much that they want to go as that they cannot stand still — like a rolling stone that cannot stop until it can go no further. For a certain sort of man, occupation is a badge of intelligence and dignity; their souls find their rest in agitation, as children do in being rocked in a cradle. They can call themselves as serviceable to their friends as they are troublesome to themselves. No one hands out his money to others, but everyone hands out his time and his life; nothing do we squander so much as those two things, and being thrifty with them would be both admirable and useful. I am of the opposite temperament. I look to myself, and what I desire I generally desire without great ardour, and I desire little; and I employ and occupy myself in the same way, sparingly and temperately. Whatever they take up, they do with the utmost will and vehemence. There are so many dangerous places that, for the sake of safety, we should glide a little lightly and superficially over the world, and not crash through it. Pleasure itself, taken in depth, is painful.
"Incedis per ignes, Suppositos cineri doloso."
["You tread on fire, hidden under deceitful ashes." --Horace, Od., ii. 1, 7.]

The Parliament of Bordeaux elected me mayor of their city while I was outside France and still further from any such thought. I asked to be excused, but my friends told me I had made a mistake in doing so, and all the more because the king had also added his command in the matter. It is an office that should be considered all the more honourable because its only salary or advantage is the bare honour of holding it. It lasts two years, but can be extended by a second election, which very rarely happens; it had happened to me, and had only happened twice before — to Monsieur de Lansac some years earlier, and recently to Monsieur de Biron, Marshal of France, in whose place I succeeded; and I left mine to Monsieur de Matignon, also Marshal of France: proud of so noble a company —
"Uterque bonus pacis bellique minister."
["Either one a good minister in peace and war." --Aeneid, xi. 658.]

Fortune wanted a hand in my promotion through one particular detail of her own, not entirely empty. Alexander disdained the ambassadors of Corinth when they came to offer him the freedom of their city; but when they went on to mention that Bacchus and Hercules were also on their roll, he thanked them graciously.

On arrival I faithfully and honestly presented myself to them as the man I find myself to be — a man without memory, without vigilance, without experience, and without vigour, but also without hatred, without ambition, without greed, and without violence — so that they could be informed of my qualities and know what they were to expect from my service. And because the knowledge they had of my late father, and the respect they had for his memory, had been their sole motive for granting me this favour, I told them plainly that I would be very sorry if anything were to make as deep an impression on me as their affairs and the concerns of their city had made on him while he held the office to which they had now preferred me. I remembered, as a boy, seeing him in his old age cruelly tormented by these public affairs, neglecting the gentle repose of his own home — to which his advancing age had reduced him for several years — neglecting the management of his own estate and his own health, and even, in a sense, despising his own life, which was in real danger of being lost on long and exhausting journeys made on their behalf. That was the man he was, and this temper of his sprang from a remarkable goodness of nature; never was there a more charitable or public-minded soul. Yet this conduct, which I commend in others, I do not love to follow myself, and not without reason.

He had learned that a man must forget himself for his neighbour, and that the particular counted for nothing compared with the general. Most of the rules and precepts of the world push in this direction — to drive us out of ourselves into the street for the benefit of public society. They thought they had accomplished a great feat by diverting and removing us from ourselves, assuming we were always too fixed there by a natural inclination, and they have said everything they could to that effect. For it is no new thing for sages to preach things not as they are but as they serve. Truth has its inconveniences and incompatibilities with us; we must often deceive in order to avoid deceiving ourselves, and shut our eyes and our understanding in order to set them right.
"Imperiti enim judicant, et qui frequenter in hoc ipsum fallendi sunt, ne errent."
["For the ignorant judge, and therefore must often be deceived, lest they should err."--Quintil., Inst. Orat., xi. 17.]

When they order us to love things three, four, or fifty degrees above ourselves, they behave like archers who, in order to hit the target, aim well above it; to make a crooked stick straight, you bend it the other way.

I believe that in the Temple of Pallas, as in all other religions, there were apparent mysteries open to the people and others, more secret and exalted, that were shown only to initiates; and it is likely that in these latter the true point of the friendship every man owes to himself was to be found — not a false friendship that makes us embrace glory, knowledge, riches, and the like as if they were limbs of our being, with primary and unmeasured affection; nor an unwise and effeminate friendship in which, as with ivy, the thing decays and ruins the wall it embraces; but a sound and well-ordered friendship, equally useful and pleasant. He who knows the duties of this friendship and practises them is truly admitted to the cabinet of the Muses, and has reached the height of human wisdom and of our happiness. Such a man, knowing exactly what he owes to himself, will see on his side that he should apply to himself the use of the world and of other men; and in order to do so, he should contribute to public society the duties and offices that belong to him. He who does not in some way live for others does not live much for himself.
"Qui sibi amicus est, scito hunc amicum omnibus esse."
["He who is his own friend, is a friend to everybody else." --Seneca, Ep., 6.]

The principal task each of us has is his own conduct, and it is for this only that we are here. Just as a man who forgot to live a virtuous and devout life himself, and thought he had discharged his duty by training others to it, would be a fool, so a man who abandons his own healthy and pleasant living to put it at the service of others takes, in my opinion, a wrong and unnatural course.
I am not saying that men should refuse, in the offices they take on, their attention, effort, eloquence, sweat, and even blood if necessary —
"Non ipse pro caris amicis Aut patria, timidus perire:"
["Himself not afraid to die for beloved friends, or for his country."--Horace, Od., iv. 9, 51.]

— but it is only on loan, and incidentally; his mind always at rest and in health, not without action, but without distress, without passion. The mere act of doing costs him so little that he acts even in his sleep; but it must be set going with judgment. The body receives the offices imposed on it just for what they are; the mind often stretches them and makes them heavier at its own expense, giving them whatever weight it pleases. Men perform similar things with very different sorts of effort and contention of will; one works just as well without the other. How many people venture themselves every day in war without much caring how things go, and throw themselves into the dangers of battles whose loss will not break their next night's sleep? And another man may sit at home, out of the very danger he would not have dared to look at, and yet be more passionately involved in the outcome of the war, and more anxious in his soul about events, than the soldier risking his blood and his life. I could have engaged myself in public employments without quitting my own business by a nail's breadth, and given myself to others without abandoning myself. This sharpness and violence of desires hinders the execution of what we undertake more than it helps it; it fills us with impatience at slow or contrary events, and with heat and suspicion against the people we have to deal with. We never carry a thing through well when it has us in its grip and leads us.
"Male cuncta ministrat Impetus."
["Impulse manages all things ill."--Statius, Thebaid, x. 704.]

He who in such matters uses only his judgment and skill proceeds more cheerfully: he fakes, he yields, he postpones quite at his ease, according to what circumstances require; he fails in his attempt without distress or grief, ready and whole for a new enterprise; he always rides with the bridle in his hand. In the man drunk on this violent and tyrannical determination, we necessarily see a great deal of imprudence and injustice; the violence of his desire carries him away; these are reckless impulses, and unless fortune greatly assists, they bear very little fruit. Philosophy directs that in revenging injuries received we should strip ourselves of anger — not so that the punishment may be less, but on the contrary so that the revenge may be better and more heavily laid on, which it holds to be hindered by all this violence. For anger not only disturbs but, on its own, wears out the arms of those who punish; this fire numbs and exhausts their force, as in haste, "festinatio tarda est" — haste trips itself up, fetters itself, and stops itself.
"Ipsa se velocitas implicat."--Seneca, Ep. 44

For example, from what I commonly see, greed has no greater obstacle than itself; the more intent and vigorous it is, the less it manages to scrape together, and it commonly grows rich sooner when it is disguised in a mask of generosity.

A very fine gentleman, and a friend of mine, came close to damaging his faculties by an excessively passionate attention and devotion to the affairs of a certain prince he served. That prince has described himself to me this way: "He foresees the weight of accidents as well as anyone, but in those for which there is no remedy he resolves at once on enduring them; in others, having taken every necessary precaution that the quickness of his mind enables him to take, he quietly waits to see what may follow." And indeed I have seen him keep a remarkable indifference and freedom of action and serenity of expression in very great and difficult affairs; I find him greater, and of greater capacity, in adversity than in prosperous fortune; his defeats are more glorious to him than his victories, and his mourning than his triumph.

Notice that even in trivial and frivolous activities — at chess, tennis, and the like — this eager and ardent engagement with passionate desire immediately throws the mind and limbs into clumsiness and disorder; a man dumbfounds and hinders himself. He who behaves more moderately, both toward gain and loss, always keeps his wits about him; the less peevish and passionate he is at play, the more advantageously and safely he plays.

Beyond all this, we hinder the mind's grasp and hold by giving it too many things to seize on; some things we should only offer to it, attach it to others, and incorporate it with still others. It can feel and discern all things, but it should feed on nothing but itself; and it should be instructed in what properly concerns itself, and in what is properly of its own substance. The laws of nature teach us what we genuinely need. After the sages have told us that no one is in need by nature, and that everyone is so by opinion, they very subtly distinguish between desires that come from her and those that come from the disorder of our own fancy: those whose end we can see are hers; those that flee before us and whose end we cannot see are our own. Poverty of goods is easily cured; poverty of the soul is incurable.
"Nam si, quod satis est homini, id satis esse potesset, Hoc sat erat: nunc, quum hoc non est, qui credimus porro Divitias ullas animum mi explere posse?"

["For if what is enough for man could be enough, it would be enough; but since it is not so, how can I believe that any wealth could give my mind content."--Lucilius ap. Nonium Marcellinum, V. sec. 98.]

Socrates, seeing a great quantity of riches, jewels, and furniture being carried in procession through his city, said: "How many things I do not desire!" Metrodorus lived on twelve ounces a day, Epicurus on less; Metrocles slept in winter outdoors among the sheep, and in summer in the cloisters of churches.
"Sufficit ad id natura, quod poscit."
["Nature suffices for what she requires."--Seneca, Ep., 90.]
Cleanthes lived by the labour of his own hands and boasted that Cleanthes, if he chose, could maintain another Cleanthes as well.

If what nature strictly and originally requires of us for the preservation of our being is too little — and indeed how little it is, and how cheaply life may be maintained, cannot be better expressed than by this consideration, that it is so little that by its very smallness it escapes the grip and shock of fortune — then let us allow ourselves a little more. Let us call every one of our habits and conditions nature; let us rate and treat ourselves by this measure; let us stretch our belongings and our accounts that far, for that far, I think, we have some excuse. Habit is a second nature, no less powerful. What is wanting to my habit, I count as wanting to me; and I would be almost as content for them to take my life as to cut me short in the way of life I have so long lived. I am no longer in condition for any great change, or for putting myself into a new and unaccustomed course, not even an improvement. The time has passed for me to become anything other than what I am; and as I should complain of any great piece of good fortune coming to me now, that it had not come in time to be enjoyed —
"Quo mihi fortunas, si non conceditur uti?"
["What good is a fortune to me, if I am not allowed to use it."--Horace, Ep., i. 5, 12.]

— so I should complain of any inner acquisition. It would be almost better never than so late to become an honest man and well fitted to live, when one has no more living to do. I, who am on the point of leaving the world, would willingly hand over to any newcomer who wanted it all the prudence I am still picking up in dealing with the world; mustard after the meat. I have no use for goods I cannot use; what good is knowledge to a man who has lost his head? It is an injury and unkindness on fortune's part to offer us presents that only inspire a just resentment that we did not have them in their due season. Guide me no further; I can walk no further. Of all the parts that make up sufficiency, patience is the most sufficient. Give the capacity for an excellent treble to the chorister whose lungs are rotten, and eloquence to a hermit exiled into the deserts of Arabia. There is no art needed to ease a fall; the end finds itself by itself at the conclusion of every affair. My world is at its end, my form is finished; I belong entirely to the past, and I am obliged to endorse it and to conform my going-out to it. I will declare here, by way of example, that the Pope's recent ten-day shortening —
[Gregory XIII., in 1582, reformed the Calendar, and, in consequence, in France they all at once passed from the 9th to the 20th December.]

— has thrown me so far off that I cannot really reconcile myself to it; I belong to the years when we kept another kind of account. So ancient and so long a habit demands my allegiance to it, so that I am forced to be a little heretical on that point — incapable of any innovation, even a corrective one. My imagination, in spite of my teeth, keeps pushing me ten days forward or backward, and murmurs constantly in my ear: "This rule concerns those who are still to begin to be." If health itself, sweet as it is, returns to me by fits, it is more to give me cause for regret than possession of it; I have no place left to keep it in. Time is leaving me, without which nothing can be possessed. Oh, how little account I should make of those great elective dignities that I see held in such esteem in the world, which are never conferred except on men who are about to take their leave of it, in which they consider not so much how well the man will discharge his trust as how short his time in it will be — from the very entry they look at the exit. In short, I am about to finish off this man, not to rebuild another. By long use, this form is in me turned into substance, and fortune into nature.

I say, then, that every one of us feeble creatures is excusable in thinking that what falls within this measure is his own; but beyond these limits there is nothing but confusion. This is the broadest extent we can grant to our own claims. The more we enlarge our needs and our possessions, the more we expose ourselves to the blows of fortune and adversity. The course of our desires ought to be circumscribed and held to a short limit of the nearest and most immediate goods; and their course ought, moreover, to be run not in a straight line that ends elsewhere, but in a circle whose two ends, by a short turn, meet and terminate in ourselves. Actions carried on without this reflection — a near and essential reflection, I mean — such as those of ambitious and greedy men, and so many others who run straight ahead, and whose course always carries them outside themselves, such actions, I say, are mistaken and diseased.
Most of our business is theatre.
"Mundus universus exercet histrioniam."

We must play our part properly, but as a part of a borrowed personage; we must not make the real essence of ourselves out of a mask and an outward appearance, nor of a strange person, our own. We cannot tell the skin from the shirt: it is enough to powder the face without powdering the chest. I see some who transform and transubstantiate themselves into as many new shapes and beings as they take on new employments; men who strut and swell into the heart and liver, and carry their official condition with them even to the privy. I cannot get them to distinguish the salutations made to themselves from those made to their commission, their retinue, or their mule.
"Tantum se fortunae permittunt, etiam ut naturam dediscant."
["They give themselves up so much to fortune, as even to unlearn nature."--Quintus Curtius, iii. 2.]

They swell up their souls and their natural way of speaking to match the height of their magisterial position. The Mayor of Bordeaux and Montaigne have always been two by a very clear separation. Because a man is a lawyer or a financier, he must not pretend to be unaware of the knavery in such callings; an honest man is not accountable for the vice or absurdity of his employment, and ought not on that account to refuse to take it up; it is the custom of his country, and there is money to be made from it; a man must live in the world and make the best of it, such as it is. But the judgment of an emperor ought to be above his empire, and to see and consider it as something foreign, external; and he ought to know how to enjoy himself apart from it, and to keep company with himself as James and Peter, regardless of what comes.

I cannot engage myself so deeply and so wholly. When my will gives me to a thing, it is not under such a violent obligation that my judgment is infected by it. In the present civil disorders of this kingdom, my own interest has not made me blind to the laudable qualities in our adversaries, or to those that are blameworthy in those on our side. Others worship everything on their own side; I, for my part, do not even excuse most things on mine. A good work loses no grace with me for being made against me. Setting aside the knot of the dispute itself, I have always kept myself in balance and pure indifference.
"Neque extra necessitates belli praecipuum odium gero;"
["Nor do I carry particular hatred beyond the necessities of war."]

For which I am pleased with myself, and all the more because I see others commonly fail in the opposite direction. Those who extend their anger and hatred beyond the dispute in question, as most men do, show that they spring from some other occasion and private cause — like a man cured of an ulcer who still has a fever, by which it appears that the ulcer had a deeper, hidden origin. The reason is that they are not concerned in the common cause because it wounds the state and the general interest, but only stung by their particular concern. That is why they are so especially fired up, and to such a degree beyond justice and public reason.
"Non tam omnia universi, quam ea, quae ad quemque pertinent, singuli carpebant."
["Everyone was not so much angry about things in general, as about those things that particularly concerned himself." --Livy, xxxiv. 36.]

I would have the advantage on our side; but if I do not get it, I will not go mad. I am heartily for the right party; but I do not want to be picked out as an especial enemy to others, beyond the general quarrel. I deeply resist this vicious form of opinion: "He is for the League because he admires the grace of Monsieur de Guise; he is impressed by the energy of the King of Navarre, therefore he is a Huguenot; he criticises this or that in the king, therefore he is seditious in his heart." And I did not grant even to the magistrate that he was right in condemning a book because it had placed a heretic among the best poets of the age. Are we not to dare say of a thief that he has a handsome leg? If a woman is a prostitute, must she necessarily smell foul? In the wisest ages, did they revoke the proud title of Capitolinus that they had conferred on Marcus Manlius as preserver of religion and public liberty, and stifle the memory of his liberality, his feats of arms, and the military honours granted to his valour, because he afterwards aspired to sovereignty against the laws of his country? If we conceive a hatred of a lawyer, will he not be allowed the next day to be eloquent? I have spoken elsewhere of the zeal that has pushed worthy men into similar errors. For my part, I can say, "Such a man does this thing badly, and another thing virtuously and well." In the same way, when affairs go badly, they would have everyone in their party be blind or a blockhead, and our judgment and conviction subservient not to the truth but to the project of our desires. I would rather lean toward the other extreme, so much do I fear being bribed by my own wishes; to which may be added that I am slightly distrustful of things I want to be true.

I have seen in my time wonders in the careless and astonishing readiness of people to let their hopes and beliefs be led and governed in whichever direction best pleased and served their leaders, despite a hundred mistakes piled one on another, despite mere dreams and fantasies. I no longer wonder at those who have been blinded and seduced by the absurdities of Apollonius and Mohammed. Their sense and understanding are entirely taken away by their passion; their discretion has no other choice than what smiles upon them and supports their cause. I had especially observed this at the beginning of our domestic troubles; the troubles since then, in imitating, have outdone it, and from that I am satisfied that it is a quality inseparable from popular errors. After the first opinion that rolls, others drive each other on like waves on the wind; a man is not a member of the body if he has it in his power to part with it, and if he does not roll along the common way. But for all that, men do an injury to the just side when they try to assist it with fraud. I have always been against that practice; it only works on weak heads. For sound ones, there are surer and more honest ways to keep their courage up and to excuse adverse events.

Heaven never saw a greater animosity than that between Caesar and Pompey, nor ever shall, and yet I notice in those great souls a great moderation toward one another; it was a jealousy of honour and command which did not carry them away into a furious and indiscreet hatred, and was without malice or slander. In their hottest exploits against one another I detect some remnants of respect and good will, and I think therefore that, if it had been possible, each of them would rather have done his business without the destruction of the other than with it. Notice how differently things went between Marius and Sylla.

We must not throw ourselves so headlong after our affections and interests. As, when I was young, I opposed the progress of love, which I felt was moving too fast on me, and took care not to let it become so pleasing as to force, captivate, and entirely surrender me to its mercy — so I do the same in every other case where my will runs on with too warm an appetite. I lean opposite to the side it is going; as I find it about to plunge and get drunk on its own wine, I avoid feeding its pleasure to the point where I could not recover it without infinite loss. Souls that through their own dullness only half-grasp things have this advantage, that they smart less under hurtful things: it is a spiritual leprosy that has the appearance of health, and a health which philosophy does not altogether despise; but we have no right to call it wisdom, as we often do. And in this manner someone once mocked Diogenes who, in the depths of winter and stark naked, was embracing a statue of snow as a test of endurance. The other, seeing him in this posture, asked, "Are you very cold?" "Not at all," replied Diogenes. "Why then," said the other, "what difficult and exemplary thing do you suppose you are doing in embracing that snow?" To take a true measure of constancy, one must necessarily know what the suffering is.

But for souls that are to meet adverse events and the injuries of fortune in their depth and sharpness, that are to weigh and taste them according to their natural weight and bitterness — let such souls show their skill in avoiding the causes and deflecting the blow. What did King Cotys do? He paid handsomely for the rich and beautiful vessel that had been presented to him, but seeing it was extremely fragile, he immediately smashed it himself, ahead of time, to prevent so easy a cause of annoyance with his servants. In the same way, I have willingly avoided all entanglements in my affairs, and never wanted my estate to border on those of my relatives or of people with whom I wanted a close friendship; for from that comes plenty of cause for ill-feeling and falling out. I used to love hazardous games of cards and dice, but gave them up long ago, only because, whatever cheerful face I put on my losses, I could not help feeling vexed inside. A man of honour, who must take an insult or a lie deeply to heart and who must not be content with some shabby apology, should avoid occasions of dispute. I shun melancholy, sour-tempered men as I would the plague, and I never meddle in matters I cannot discuss without emotion and concern, unless duty compels me.
"Melius non incipient, quam desinent."
["It is better never to begin than to have to leave off." --Seneca, Ep., 72.]
The safest course, then, is to prepare oneself beforehand for the situation.

I know very well that some wise men have taken the other route, and have not feared to grapple with and engage many subjects to the utmost. These men are confident in their own strength, under which they shield themselves in any setback, making their patience wrestle and contend with disaster.
"Velut rupes, vastum quae prodit in aequor, Obvia ventorum furiis, expostaque ponto, Vim cunctam atque minas perfert coelique marisque; Ipsa immota manens."
["As a rock, which juts into the vast ocean, exposed to the fury of the winds and the raging sea, endures the whole force and threats of sky and sea, itself unmoved."--Virgil, Aeneid, x. 693.]

Let us not attempt these examples; we shall never come up to them. They set themselves resolutely, and without agitation, to watch the ruin of their country, which possessed and commanded all their will: that is too much, and too hard a task for our more ordinary souls. Cato gave up the noblest life that ever was on this account; we lesser spirits must run from the storm as far as we can; we must provide for feeling, not for endurance, and dodge blows we cannot meet. Zeno, seeing Chremonides, a young man he was fond of, come up to sit beside him, suddenly jumped up, and when Cleanthes asked why he did so, said: "I hear that physicians especially prescribe rest, and forbid disturbance, in all swellings." Socrates does not say: "Do not surrender to the charms of beauty; stand your ground, and do everything you can to resist it." "Flee from it," he says; "avoid the sight and encounter of it, as you would of a powerful poison that shoots its arrows and wounds at a distance." And his fine pupil, inventing or recounting — in my opinion rather recounting than inventing — the rare perfections of the great Cyrus, makes him distrustful of his own strength to resist the charms of the divine beauty of that illustrious Panthea, his captive, and so he commits the visiting and keeping of her to another, who could not have so much liberty as himself. And the Holy Spirit, likewise:
"Ne nos inducas in tentationem."
["Lead us not into temptation."--St. Matthew, vi. 13.]

We do not pray that our reason should not be combated and overcome by lust, but that it should not even be tried by it — that we should not be brought into a state where we even have to face the approaches, solicitations, and temptations of sin; and we beg Almighty God to keep our consciences quiet, fully and perfectly delivered from all dealings with evil.

Those who say that they have reason for their vengeful passion, or for some other troublesome agitation of mind, often speak truly as things now stand, but not as they were. They speak to us when the causes of their error are by themselves being fed and pushed forward; but go backwards — trace those causes back to their beginning — and there you will stop them in their tracks. Will their faults be less for being longer-lived? Will an unjust beginning make a just sequel? Whoever desires the good of his country, as I do, without fretting or wasting himself, will be troubled, but not faint, to see it threatening either its own ruin or a no less ruinous survival; a poor vessel, tossed and steered by waves, winds, and pilot toward conflicting destinations!
"In tam diversa magister Ventus et unda trahunt."

He who does not gape after the favour of princes as after something he cannot live without is not much disturbed by the coolness of their reception and demeanour, or by the inconstancy of their wills. He who does not brood over his children or his honours with a slavish attachment does not stop living comfortably enough after their loss. He who does good principally for his own satisfaction will not be much troubled to see men judge his actions contrary to their merit. A quarter ounce of patience will provide sufficiently against such inconveniences. I find ease in this prescription, redeeming myself at the start as cheaply as I can; and by this means I have escaped much trouble and many difficulties. With very little fuss I stop the first outburst of my emotions, and I leave the subject that is beginning to be bothersome before it carries me away. He who does not stop the start will never be able to stop the course; he who cannot keep them out will never get them out once they are in; and he who cannot reach the beginning will never reach the end of it all. Nor will he bear the fall who cannot stand the shock.
"Etenim ipsae se impellunt, ubi semel a ratione discessum est; ipsaque sibi imbecillitas indulget, in altumque provehitur imprudens, nec reperit locum consistendi."

["For they throw themselves headlong once they have departed from reason; and weakness indulges itself, and from lack of prudence is carried out into deep water, and finds no place to take shelter."--Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., iv. 18.]
I am alert in good time to the little breezes that begin to sing and whistle inside me, the forerunners of the storm.
"Ceu flamina prima Cum deprensa fremunt sylvis et caeca volutant Murmura, venturos nautis prodentia ventos."
["As the first breezes, caught in the woods, rumble and roll their hidden murmurs, announcing to sailors the winds to come."--Aeneid, x. 97.]

How often have I done myself a clear injustice in order to avoid the risk of having a worse one done me by the judges, after years of harassment, dirty and vile practices, more hateful to my nature than fire or the rack?
"Convenit a litibus, quantum licet, et nescio an paulo plus etiam quam licet, abhorrentem esse: est enim non modo liberale, paululum nonnunquam de suo jure decedere, sed interdum etiam fructuosum."

["A man should shrink from lawsuits as much as he can, and perhaps a little more than he should; for it is not only generous, but sometimes even profitable, to give up a little of one's own right."--Cicero, De Offic., ii. 18.]

If we were wise, we should rejoice and boast, as I one day heard a young gentleman of good family very innocently do, that his mother had lost her case — as if it had been a cough or a fever, or something tiresome to keep. Even the favours that fortune might have given me through kinship or acquaintance with those who have sovereign authority in such matters, I have very conscientiously and carefully avoided employing to the prejudice of others, or to push my own claims beyond their true right. In the end, I have so far succeeded in my efforts — and I may happily say it — that I am to this day a virgin in matters of lawsuits, though I have been offered fair ones, and with a fully just title, had I been willing to listen; and a virgin in quarrels too. I have nearly passed through a long life without any offence of any consequence, either active or passive, or even hearing a worse word spoken than my own name: a rare favour of heaven.

Our greatest agitations have ridiculous springs and causes. What ruin did our last Duke of Burgundy bring on himself over a cartload of sheepskins! And was not the engraving of a seal the first and chief cause of the greatest convulsion that this machine of the world has ever undergone? For Pompey and Caesar were only the later phases and continuation of two earlier men; and I have seen in my own time the wisest heads in this kingdom assembled with great ceremony, and at the public expense, to negotiate treaties and settlements whose actual decision meanwhile depended entirely on the ladies' cabinet council and the inclination of some scrap of a woman.

The poets understood this well when they set all Greece and Asia to fire and sword over an apple. Look — there is a man risking his life and honour on the chance of his rapier and dagger; ask him to tell you the cause of the quarrel; he cannot do it without blushing, the occasion is so silly and frivolous.

A small thing will get you into it, but once you are embarked, every cord pulls; large supplies are then required, more demanding and more important. How much easier it is not to go in than to get out! Now we should go about it the opposite way from the reed, which at its first springing puts forth a long and straight shoot, and afterwards, as if winded, runs into thick and frequent joints and knots, as so many pauses showing that it has lost its first vigour and firmness. We had better begin gently and coolly, and save our breath and our vigorous efforts for the height and stress of the business. We govern affairs at their beginnings, and have them in our power; but afterwards, once they are under way, it is they that govern us, and we have to follow them.

Yet I do not mean to say that this principle has freed me from all difficulty, or that I have not often had enough to do to curb and restrain my passions; they are not always to be governed according to the measure of the occasion, and often have very sharp and violent entries. Still, good fruit and benefit can be gathered from them — except by those who in doing well are not satisfied with any benefit if reputation is missing; for in truth such an effect is valued only by oneself; you are more content, but not more esteemed, because you reformed yourself before you got into the whirl of the dance, or before the provoking matter was even in sight. Yet not only here, but in all other duties of life, the path of those who aim at honour is very different from the path taken by those whose aim is order and reason. I see some who rashly and furiously rush into the lists and cool off in the course. As Plutarch says of those who, through false shame, are soft and ready to grant whatever is asked of them, and are afterwards just as ready to break their word and to retract — so a man who enters a quarrel lightly is likely to leave it just as lightly. The same difficulty that keeps me from entering it would, once I was hot and engaged in the quarrel, drive me to maintain it with great obstinacy and resolve. It is the tyranny of habit: once a man has engaged himself, he must go through with it or die. "Take on coolly," said Bias, "but pursue with ardour." For lack of prudence, men fall into a lack of courage, which is even more intolerable.

Most settlements of the quarrels of our day are shameful and false; we only seek to save appearances, and meanwhile betray and disavow our true intentions; we paper over the fact. We know very well how we said the thing, and in what sense we said it, and the company knows it, and our friends, to whom we wished to make our advantage clear, understand it well enough too. It is at the cost of our frankness and of the honour of our courage that we disown our thoughts and take refuge in falsehoods to patch things up. We give ourselves the lie in order to excuse the lie we have given another. You are not to consider whether your word or action might admit some other interpretation; it is your own true and sincere interpretation, your real meaning in what you said or did, that you are from then on to maintain, whatever it costs. Men speak to your virtue and your conscience, which are not things to be put under a mask; let us leave these pitiful expedients and dodges to the jugglers of the law. The excuses and reparations that I see every day made and given for indiscretions seem to me more shameful than the indiscretion itself. It would be better to insult your opponent a second time than to insult yourself by giving him so unmanly a satisfaction. You stood up to him in your heat and anger, and now you would flatter and pacify him in your cooler and better sense; and by that you lay yourself lower and at the feet of the man you previously pretended to tower over. I find nothing a gentleman can say so wicked in him as that unsaying what he has said is dishonourable, when the unsaying is extracted from him by pressure — since stubbornness is more excusable in a man of honour than cowardice. Passions are as easy for me to evade as they are hard for me to moderate.
"Exscinduntur facilius animo, quam temperantur."
["They are more easily uprooted from the mind than governed in it."]

Whoever cannot reach the noble Stoic impassivity, let him take cover in the lap of this common dullness of mine; what they achieved by virtue, I train myself to do by temperament. The middle region harbours storms and tempests; the two extremes — of philosophers and peasants — meet in tranquillity and happiness.

"Felix, qui potuit rerum cognoscere causas, Atque metus omnes et inexorabile fatum Subjecit pedibus, strepitumque Acherontis avari! Fortunatus et ille, Deos qui novit agrestes, Panaque, Sylvanumque senem, Nymphasque sorores!"

["Happy is he who has been able to learn the causes of things, and has placed under his feet all fears and unyielding fate, and the noise of greedy Acheron: blessed too is he who knows the country gods, and Pan, and old Sylvanus, and the sister nymphs."--Virgil, Georg., ii. 490.]

The births of all things are weak and tender, and so we should have our eyes fixed on beginnings; for just as in its infancy the danger is not perceived, so when it has grown up the remedy is just as hard to find. I should have met a million crosses every day, harder to swallow in the pursuit of ambition, than it has been hard for me to curb the natural inclination that drew me toward it.
"Jure perhorrui Late conspicuum tollere verticem."
["I justly feared to raise my head conspicuously high." --Horace, Od., iii. 16, 18.]

All public actions are open to uncertain and varied interpretations, because too many heads judge of them. Some say of this civic employment of mine — and I am willing to say a word or two about it, not because it is worth so much, but to give an account of my manners in such matters — that I conducted myself in it as a man too sluggish and of a languid temperament; and they have some colour for what they say. I tried to keep my mind and my thoughts at rest.
"Cum semper natura, tum etiam aetate jam quietus;"
["As being always quiet by nature, so also now by age." --Cicero, De Petit. Consul., c. 2.]

And if they sometimes lash out under some rough and sensitive impression, it is truthfully without my consent. Yet from this natural heaviness of mine, men should not conclude a total incapacity in me (for lack of care and lack of sense are two very different things), and still less any unkindness or ingratitude toward that corporation which used every means in their power to oblige me, both before they knew me and afterwards; and they did much more for me in choosing me a second time than in conferring the honour on me at first. I wish them every imaginable good; and assuredly, if there had been occasion, there is nothing I would have spared for their service; I did for them as I would have done for myself. They are a good, warlike, generous people, but capable of obedience and discipline, and of whom the best use can be made if they are well led. They also say that my administration passed without leaving any mark or trace. Good! They further accuse my abstention at a time when almost everyone was convicted of doing too much. I am eager to act where my will spurs me on; but this very eagerness is an enemy to perseverance. Let anyone who wants to use me in my own way employ me in affairs where vigour and freedom are required, where a direct, short, and even hazardous conduct is necessary; I may do something. But if it must be long, subtle, laborious, artificial, and intricate, he had better call in somebody else. Not all important offices are necessarily difficult; I came prepared to do rougher work, had there been great occasion; for it is in my power to do something more than I do, or than I like to do. I did not, to my knowledge, leave out anything that my duty really required. I easily forgot those duties that ambition mixes with duty and disguises with its label; those are the ones that, for the most part, fill the eyes and ears and give men the most satisfaction; not the thing but the appearance contents them; if they hear no noise, they think men are asleep. My temperament is no friend to commotion; I could settle a disturbance without commotion, and chastise a disorder without being disorderly myself; if I need anger and excitement, I borrow it and put it on. My manners are languid, more faint than sharp. I do not condemn a magistrate who sleeps, provided the people in his charge sleep as well as he does; in that case the laws sleep too. For my part, I commend a gliding, settled, and silent life.
"Neque submissam et abjectam, neque se efferentem;"
["Neither submissive and abject, nor obtrusive." --Cicero, De Offic., i. 34]
My fortune wants it so. I am descended from a family that has lived without splendour or noise and, time out of mind, particularly proud of a reputation for honesty.

Our people nowadays are so trained up to bustle and show that good nature, moderation, equability, constancy, and other such quiet and obscure qualities are no longer thought of or noticed. Rough bodies make themselves felt; smooth ones are handled imperceptibly; sickness is felt, health little or not at all, any more than the oils that soothe us, compared with the pains for which we are soothed. It is acting for one's own reputation and profit, not for the public good, to refer to the public square what could be done in the council chamber, or to noonday what could have been done the night before; or to be jealous to do oneself what one's colleague can do as well as you; some surgeons of Greece used to perform their operations on platforms in plain sight of the people, to attract more practice and more profit. They think that good rules cannot be understood except by the sound of a trumpet. Ambition is not a vice of small people or of such modest means as ours. Someone said to Alexander: "Your father will leave you a great dominion, easy and at peace"; this young man was envious of his father's victories and the justice of his rule; he would not have enjoyed the empire of the world in ease and peace. Alcibiades, in Plato, would rather die young, beautiful, rich, noble, and learned, with all this at the very peak, than fall short of such a condition; this disease is, perhaps, excusable in so strong and so full a soul. But when wretched, dwarfish little souls flatter and deceive themselves, and think to spread their fame for having given a correct judgment in some matter, or maintained discipline at the guard of a city gate, the more they think to raise their heads, the more they show their tails. This petty doing-good has neither body nor life; it vanishes in the first mouth, and goes no further than from one street to another. Brag of it by all means to your son or your servant, like the old fellow who, having no other audience for his praises or witness to his valour, boasted to his chambermaid, crying: "O Perrette, what a fine, clever man you have for a master!" At worst, talk of it to yourself, like a councillor of my acquaintance who, having disgorged a whole cartful of legal jargon with great heat and equal folly, on coming out of the council chamber to relieve himself, was heard quite contentedly muttering between his teeth:
"Non nobis, domine, non nobis, sed nomini tuo da gloriam."
["Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto Thy name be the glory." --Psalm cxiii. 1.]
He who gets it from nobody else, let him pay himself out of his own purse.

Fame is not prostituted that cheaply. The rare and exemplary actions to which it is due would not put up with the company of this enormous crowd of petty daily performances. Marble may exalt your titles all you please, for having repaired a yard of wall or cleaned out a public sewer — but men of sense will not. Renown does not follow every good deed unless novelty and difficulty are joined to it; in fact even mere esteem, according to the Stoics, is not due to every action that springs from virtue; nor will they grant bare thanks to a man who, out of temperance, abstains from a bleary old crone. Those who have known the admirable qualities of Scipio Africanus deny him the glory Panaetius attributes to him, of being incorruptible by gifts — a glory not so much his as that of his age. We have pleasures suitable to our station; let us not lay claim to those of grandeur; our own are more natural, and so much more solid and sure as they are lower. If not for conscience's sake, then at least for ambition's sake, let us reject ambition; let us scorn that thirst for honour and renown that is so low and beggarly that it makes us beg it of all sorts of people:
"Quae est ista laus quae possit e macello peti?"
["What praise is that which can be picked up in the market-place (meat market)?"--Cicero, De Fin., ii. 15.]

— by base means, and at however cheap a rate; it is dishonour to be honoured in this way. Let us learn to be no greedier of glory than we are capable of glory. To be puffed up with every action that is innocent or useful is only for those for whom such things are extraordinary and rare; they will value such things at what they cost them. The more noise a good effect makes, the more I subtract from its goodness, suspecting that it was performed more for the noise than on account of the goodness; once on display in the market, it is half sold. Those actions have much more grace and lustre that slip from the hand of the doer carelessly and without noise, and that some honest man afterwards finds out and lifts from the shade to bring it into the light on its own account:
"Mihi quidem laudabiliora videntur omnia, quae sine venditatione, et sine populo teste fiunt,"
["To me, indeed, all things seem more laudable which are done without ostentation, and without the people as witness." --Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., ii. 26.]
— says the most ostentatious man who ever lived.

I had only to conserve and to continue, which are silent and unnoticed effects; innovation is full of glitter, but it is forbidden in this age, when we are under pressure and have nothing to defend ourselves against but novelties. Refraining from doing is often as generous as doing, but it is less in the spotlight, and the little good I have in me is of this kind. In short, the occasions during this employment of mine were in league with my temperament, and I am heartily grateful to them for it. Is there anyone who wishes to be sick in order to see his physician at work? And would not a physician deserve a whipping who wished the plague among us so he could put his art into practice? I have never had that wicked humour, common as it is, to wish that troubles and disorders in this city should magnify and honour my government; I have always wholeheartedly contributed everything I could to its tranquillity and ease.

He who will not thank me for the order, the gentle and silent calm that has accompanied my administration, cannot, however, deprive me of the share that belongs to me under the heading of my good fortune. And I am of such a make that I would as willingly be lucky as wise, and would rather owe my successes purely to the favour of Almighty God than to anything I did myself. I had sufficiently announced to the world my unfitness for such public offices, but I have something in me even worse than this incapacity itself, which is that I am not greatly displeased about it, and that I do not work hard to cure it, given the course of life I have set for myself.

Nor have I satisfied myself in this employment; but I have come very near to what I expected from my own performance, and have far exceeded what I promised those I had to deal with: for I tend to promise something less than what I am able to do, and than what I hope to make good. I assure myself that I have left no offence or hatred behind me; as to leaving regret or longing for me among them, I at least know very well that I never much aimed at it.
"Mene huic confidere monstro! Mene salis placidi vultum, fluctusque quietos Ignorare?"
["Should I place confidence in this monster? Should I be ignorant of the look of that seeming-calm sea and those now-quiet waves?" --Virgil, Aeneid, V. 849.]
